# Prescriptive lessons — dirk-laukens × beginners-guide

## maj7

Laukens treats maj7 as the resolution target of the ii–V–I and teaches it as one of five moveable CAGED-correspondent shapes named by the red-dot root. He additionally assigns it two distinct scale prescriptions: the major blues scale (no 7th, so no clash) and, in bebop blues, the maj7 quality marks the tonic as Bird Blues rather than standard blues. The major blues scale's 7th-free structure is the mechanism that makes it safe across both dom7 and maj7 without reharmonizing.

- [ch.1 p.10] maj7 introduced as one of five essential moveable shapes; red-dot root names the chord, thumb on bass, fingers 1–3 on upper voices for string-6-root voicings. All five shapes map to CAGED positions (ch.3 p.66).
- [ch.4 p.83] Major blues scale (major pentatonic + b3) prescribed for soloing over maj7 in major-key contexts; absence of the 7th prevents clash with the chord's major-7 quality, making the scale safe over both G7 and Gmaj7 without adjustment.
- [ch.6 p.172] Bird Blues defined by replacing the standard I7 tonic with Imaj7; maj7 is the explicit harmonic marker distinguishing bebop blues from standard blues, not merely an embellishment.

---

## dom7

Laukens gives dom7 more scale prescriptions than any other quality: Mixolydian for unaltered contexts, phrygian dominant (fifth mode of harmonic minor) as the first-choice bebop sound for V7 and V7alt, Lydian Dominant when the tritone sub is played, and minor/major b3–3 mixing for a blues feel. In standard blues, dom7 is also the normative tonic quality of all three basic chords—not just the V. Sus-chord substitution and tritone substitution are taught as bar-level comping decisions, not just theoretical options.

- [ch.1 p.10 / ch.6 p.158–159] dom7 is one of five essential moveable shapes and the normative tonic of standard blues; all three basic blues chords (I, IV, V) are dom7; lead-sheet symbols may be embellished with 9ths, 13ths, and 6ths in comping.
- [ch.5 p.101] Phrygian dominant scale (fifth mode of harmonic minor) prescribed as the first-choice soloing sound over V7 and V7alt in bebop; this is stated as a rule-level prescription, not a suggestion.
- [ch.5 p.105 / ch.6 p.169] Tritone substitution: play any 7th chord a tritone away in place of the original dom7; shared 3rd and 7th (e.g., C7 and F#7 both contain E and Bb) validate the swap; bar-specific applications given for jazz blues (e.g., bar 10: Bb7 in place of E7).
- [ch.5 p.112] Mixolydian mode prescribed as the default scalar color for unaltered dom7; demonstrated via double-stop soloing over a pedal tone using A Mixolydian.
- [ch.6 p.178] Sus chord prescribed as a comping technique to delay and add motion to a dominant chord; offered both as a bar-specific instruction (bar 10 of blues example) and as a general dom7 comping rule.
- [ch.6 p.182] Mixing b3 (minor blues scale) with natural 3 (Mixolydian) over dom7 prescribed as the core technique for a bluesy jazz sound; mixing F minor blues scale with F Mixolydian is the named method.

---

## dom7b9

Laukens traces dom7b9 to two sources: Count Basie's VI7b9 as a secondary dominant innovation preceding the ii chord, and harmonic minor applied over V7alt generating the b9 as a natural scale degree. Both lessons converge on the prescription that harmonic minor is the appropriate scale for any b9-altered dominant context.

- [ch.6 p.164] VI7b9 identified as a Count Basie innovation in jazz blues, functioning as a secondary dominant with added b9 tension in bar 8 preceding the ii chord.
- [ch.6 p.184 / ch.4 p.87] Harmonic minor prescribed for soloing over dom7b9; the G harmonic minor scale over D7 generates a 7b9 sound as a natural scale degree; tonic harmonic minor over V7alt "create[s] a V7(b9,b13) sound"—b9 alteration is built into the scale, not added.

---

## dom7alt

Laukens gives two complementary routes to soloing over dom7alt, both sourced from harmonic minor but approached from different modal entry points: tonic harmonic minor (from the Im tonic root) and phrygian dominant (from the V root, the fifth mode of the same harmonic minor). A third route, Lydian Dominant, is prescribed specifically when the tritone sub is used in place of the original V7alt.

- [ch.4 p.87 / ch.5 p.101] Tonic harmonic minor prescribed for V7alt in a minor ii–V–I; for Autumn Leaves B7alt, use the tonic (G) harmonic minor scale. Phrygian dominant is the same harmonic minor source heard from the V root—both prescriptions derive from one scale, approached from different modal starting points.
- [ch.6 p.183] Lydian Dominant prescribed when the tritone sub is played in place of a V7alt; B Lydian Dominant = F Altered scale, so the tritone sub and its Lydian Dominant produce the same altered color as the original chord's altered scale.

---

## min7

Laukens covers min7 across four distinct roles: ii chord arpeggio work (voice-led by proximity), Im7 in minor ii–V–I (melodic minor with raised 7th as expressive tension), modal Dorian tonic (each chord demands its own scale), and Pat Metheny–style three-note-per-string legato phrasing. The melodic minor raised-7th prescription is explicitly framed as an expressive choice the player experiments with rather than a mandatory application.

- [ch.1 p.10 / ch.3 p.54–55, 59] min7 introduced as one of five essential moveable shapes; Am7 is the anchor example for two arpeggio patterns (5th/4th skips; groups of three notes); all shapes are moveable and CAGED-correspondent.
- [ch.4 p.89–90] Melodic minor (raised 7th) prescribed for Im7 in a minor ii–V–I; raised 7th creates deliberate tension; player is instructed to experiment with placement of that interval rather than apply it mechanically throughout.
- [ch.2 p.34] Modal min7 chords (Maiden Voyage) treated as Dorian tonic centers; each of the four key-center changes across the 32-bar form requires a fresh Dorian scale assignment—a direct application of the chord-specific scale-change rule.
- [ch.5 p.139] Three-note-per-string legato lines prescribed for min7 soloing, citing Pat Metheny; add as many hammer-ons per string as possible to build fluid phrasing over Dm7.

---

## min7b5

Laukens assigns min7b5 a dual identity: structurally, it is one of the five essential chord qualities (moveable CAGED shapes, small Roman numeral notation); functionally, it occupies the ii position in minor ii–V–I. The scale prescription—natural minor / Aeolian—is chosen partly for its shared-root convenience across the whole minor ii–V–I complex, reducing fingering changes.

- [ch.4 p.85] Natural minor (Aeolian, sixth mode of major) prescribed for soloing over the half-diminished ii chord in a minor ii–V–I; Autumn Leaves F#m7b5 is the example; shared-root strategy reduces fingering complexity across the minor ii–V–I.
- [ch.1 p.10 / ch.7 p.192] min7b5 established as one of five essential jazz chord qualities; occupies the ii position in minor ii–V–I; notated with small Roman numeral (vii°/ii°) encoding its minor/diminished quality; all CAGED-correspondent moveable shapes apply.

---

## dim7

Laukens uses dim7 in four distinct ways, and crucially names one memorization-reduction rule unique to this quality: its symmetry means only two grips cover all positions. Beyond comping, the "3 to 9 arpeggio" prescription—dim7 from the 3rd of any 7th chord—is singled out as "essential learning for any bebop guitarist," giving dim7 a cross-quality substitution role well beyond its own chord sound.

- [ch.6 p.164] #IVdim7 identified as a Count Basie innovation used as a chromatic passing chord between I7 and IV7 in jazz blues (bars 2 and 6); dim7 functions as a passing substitute, not a standalone tonic or dominant.
- [ch.3 p.70] Only two grips needed for all dim7 chord and arpeggio shapes due to structural symmetry; the only chord quality in the book that receives a memorization-reduction prescription based on symmetry.
- [ch.5 p.104] "3 to 9 arpeggio": play a dim7 arpeggio from the 3rd of any 7th chord to outline 3–5–b7–b9 of that chord; named "an essential learning for any bebop guitarist"; the dim7 shape is borrowed to inject b9 color into a dom7 context.
- [ch.6 p.178] Contrary motion prescribed for voice leading into a dim7 chord (IV9 → #IVdim7): bass moves upward (C to C#) while the inner voice moves downward (D to C#); contrary motion explicitly named as the preferred technique.
